edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimittere pristina gesta: Luxurias vita, quoniam labor imminet armis. Imperio regis omni virtute parendum, Tempora postrema si vis pertingere laeta. Ille bonus miles, semper exspecta fruenda; Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino mitte, Ut tuo praeposito cottidie praesto sis, ante Solicitus esto, matutinus signa revise. Cum videris bellum, agonia sume propinqua. Haec gloria regis, militem videre paratum; Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum. Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli: Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.
pass_a_gloss: When you have given the name of a soldier, you are held by a bridle. Begin then to dismiss former deeds: a life of luxury, because labor with arms is imminent. You must obey the command of the King with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times happily. He is a good soldier, who always expects things to be enjoyed; do not flatter yourself, completely dismiss idleness, so that you may be present daily for your commander, be solicitous beforehand, revise the signs in the morning. When you see war, take up nearby agony. This is the glory of the King, to see the soldier prepared; the King is present, who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts, he rejoices in the victory, and suspends his own attendant to be dedicated. You, moreover, do not spare yourself in regard to Belial: be more energetic, so that he may give fame in exchange for death.

pass_b_english: Once you take the name of a soldier, a bridle holds you. So begin now to put off your former deeds: a life of luxury, because labor with arms is imminent. You must obey the King's command with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times happily. A good soldier always expects rewards; do not flatter yourself, dismiss idleness completely, so that you may stand ready daily for your commander — be anxious beforehand, review the standards at dawn. When you see war, take up the agony at hand. This is the King's glory: to see the soldier prepared. The King is present, who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts, he rejoices in the victory, and looks upon his own attendant to be dedicated. You, moreover, do not spare yourself against Belial: be more energetic, so that he may give you fame in exchange for death.

review.notes: Pass A fails to translate 'Suspicit' correctly, translating it as 'suspends' (likely confusing it with 'suspende' or similar), whereas the Latin 'Suspicit' means 'looks upon' or 'looks up at'. Pass B correctly identifies 'looks upon', but Pass A's error creates a contradiction between the two passes regarding the King's action. Furthermore, Pass A translates 'fruenda' as 'things to be enjoyed' (a gerundive/participle sense) but misses the specific nuance of 'rewards' or 'fruit' found in the context of a soldier's expectation, though 'things to be enjoyed' is a literal gloss. The primary failure is the mistranslation of 'Suspicit' in Pass A: 'suspends his own attendant to be dedicated' vs 'looks upon his own attendant to be dedicated'.
reasons: Pass A mistranslates 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' as 'suspends his own attendant to be dedicated', whereas 'Suspicit' means 'looks upon' or 'looks up at'. Pass B correctly renders this as 'looks upon his own attendant to be dedicated'.

review.notes: The Latin text is correctly identified as 'Instructions LIII' from the specified edition. The translation preserves the original meaning, including the correct use of terms like 'freno' as 'bridle' and 'satellem' as 'attendant'. The title 'Christian Soldier's Conduct' accurately reflects the content of the passage. All source paragraphs are accounted for, and no errors in fidelity, completeness, or doctrinal accuracy are found.
